  - **Scenario 2: Y decided worse, partly because of this entry.**
    - The base's text has no dating test. Y argued only that P-26 "does not apply", since the specification has had the idiom since 2009 (`var-ref.tex:63-69`). It weighed Naden's date without a rule to apply it.
    - X's text "asks that 'later' be a date checked against the texts". X applied it, and that was better.
    - The fact that would have prevented Y's lapse: a prelude design counts as the team's later word only if it is later than the library's text and no later text of the team's on the language contradicts it. Naden's write-up is dated 2012-08-31, after Steele's edits (`self-typed-bodies-judgement.md:23`).
  - **Scenario 3: neither reader decided worse.** The base's list, "the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010", did not lead Y to (a). Y wrote "P-43 and P-26 speak of the number types".
- **POSITIONS 42** (scenario 1). It helped both readers.
  - Y used "The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types" against (a). It used "The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure" against (b).
  - X used the same two points.

That did not make X decide worse: X checked, and treated the defect as unrecorded. A reader who trusted the citation would have skipped the row. The entry cites a row before the row exists.

A range over another integer type is a static error." did not become a precedent for either. Both told the case apart as a fixable defect, not a limit. That ground would admit a rule of the language for a real limit, which the key does not allow. Neither relied on it alone.

  - **Scenario 2: Y decided worse, partly because of this entry.** The base's "the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types" is a permission with no test. X's text "states when a prelude design binds the one library", and X applied its two cases, which was better. The preventing fact is the same dated test as under POSITIONS 26.

content.content:
59:- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

88:- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

65:- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's later code bounds the element of both of its lexicographic traits by a total order (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`; P-26, the team's later word outweighs its early text), and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.

66:- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

69:- P-158 **A member that an api writes `abstract` is declared in the component that exports the api.** The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. The compiled export check refuses a component that leaves one out, and the checker then checks that each object defines it. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and the team's export check of 2012 enforces it; by P-26, on the team's later word, that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification asks for no body there, not for no declaration (`Specification/basic/components/apis.tex`, "Component and API Identity"). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816).

24:- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper (F-166). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.

34:- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. How the checker comes to accept the library, its first step and the order of the work, was left to a plan for him, which he approved (P-33).

25:- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.

40:- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

84:- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.

39:- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure: while it uses the compiler's prelude, it bounds such a parameter by `Object`, and so refuses a generic instantiated at a tuple (row 412).

<!-- The foundations review's POSITIONS rewrite and its trap test, 2026-10-26: which thirteen entries were rewritten after the Fable judgement and how, the coordinator's edits after the judges, the trap test's result (the new texts 12 of 12, today's 10 of 12, blind Opus grading), where the old texts failed, the key's slips, and what is still owed before the texts enter POSITIONS. -->

# The POSITIONS rewrite after the foundations review, and its trap test

## What was rewritten

- **The entries:** P-26, P-37, P-43, P-42, P-7 and P-158 (chunk c1); P-33, P-12, P-59, P-17, P-84, P-85 and P-58 (chunk c2). The target was the judgement's section 7 (`judgement.md`): what each new text must make the coordinator do. The curator approved the rewrite and its trap test on 2026-10-26 at 07:42 and 07:48 UTC.
- **The run:** the clarity workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/`), Workflow run `wf_36572c60-a05`, with a run brief of its own passed as `args.extra`: the judgement's section 7 as the target; the three layers defined once, in P-26; "later" as a date; one home for each rule (the general rule for counting the team's code in P-26, its application to the compiler's prelude in P-37); each new ground marked "from the judgement, for his yes"; the open answers of the curator written under their defaults, each dependent sentence listed. A headless Opus writer, an Opus cold reader with only the worker skill, an Opus checker, the writer's fix round, a second cold read, and an Opus judge per chunk. Both judges applied every entry, none held.
- **The coordinator's edits after the judges** (`evidence/rewrite/combined.apply`, which holds the thirteen texts as tested): three "Still to build" lines cut (P-42, P-158, P-33), since an entry holds no plan or status (the coordinator skill, `references/record.md`); P-42's tuple-typed dotted method named as row 832; P-158's pointer to row 816 given its subject; P-58's "which climb batch 23 begins" cut.
- **The fourteen** in the texts: the distance stage's twelve components (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh:85-87`) and the two that `List` imports, `CovariantCollection` and `OneShotFlag` (`Library/List.fss:13`, `:15`). The judgements of 2026-10-24 and 2026-10-26 write "thirteen", a miscount.
- **Corrected after the trap test, which did not cover it:** P-158's ground. The rewrite read the specification's export rules as ambiguous on whether a component declares an abstract member. They are not: a component's trait or object contains a satisfying declaration "for each field declaration and non-abstract method declaration in the exported declaration", and may give an abstract one a concrete declaration (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:372-385`, the same in the Working Draft), the rule that the team's export checker quoted in 2009 (`80d8c678a`). So P-158 does not rest on the second case of P-37's rule; its ground is the team's later work, the export check that from 2009-05-08 refused a component trait with fewer members than its api's (`ac0d41de0`, Sukyoung Ryu, three months after the checker that quoted the rule), by P-26, with the specification revised to follow it. Climb batch 22c's planner found this (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-22c.md`, question 3). `combined.apply` holds the corrected P-158 and P-37 (`0230803b6`).
- **The run's files:** `evidence/rewrite/c1/` and `c2/` (each chunk's proposals with the source of each sentence, the cold reads, the check, the judgement and the queue items).

## The trap test

- **Its form:** the record-test kit (`explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/README.md`) on four scenarios written before the new texts existed (`evidence/trap-test/questions.md`, `key.md`; scenario 2's key reconciled with the judgement's section 3 at `837cabc32`). Two detached worktrees at `bedc80b01`, before the routing of the review's findings, with `explorations/reviews/foundations/`, the conversation note `explorations/conversations/02-phase3-exit-foundations.md` and the kit's own files removed; one kept today's entries, the other had the thirteen texts applied. One Opus reader in each, acting as the coordinating session (`fortress-repo`, then `coordinator`). One blind Opus grader.
- **The result:** the new texts 12 of 12 (decision 8 of 8, sources 4 of 4); today's entries 10 of 12 (decision 6 of 8, sources 4 of 4). Scenarios 1 and 3 scored the same; both readers refused the trap's invitation there.
- **Where today's entries fell short** (`evidence/trap-test/grades.md`, sections 2 and 4):
  - Scenario 2, the order traits' `comprises T`: the reader dropped the rung on P-27's library practice and kept way 5 open for a probe and an ask, with Naden's later date in hand but no rule that made the dated later word decide. The new P-37 and P-26 gave that rule.
  - Scenario 4, a `CompilerSystem` kept as the compiled path's `System`: the reader refused the rung, but offered a `CompilerSystem` bridge as an option of its ask, since today's P-37 gives no reason for one library. The new P-37 carries the curator's reason: no port of walk's library into the compiler's.
- **The key's slips, found by the grader** (none turns a score): `System`'s two errors may be cleared in the names batch as well as before it (`reviews/phase3-exit/judgement.md` 5.2, item 8; `CLIMB-BATCH-23.md:44`); no gated compiled test can see the one-library `case` branch before the switch-over, so its test is a probe with walk's twin; the bound `Any` widens the tuple-typed dotted method's reach (`b.wrap[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]`, `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md:64`); "the coordinator settles the finding itself" against `fortress-repo`'s `exploring.md:7`, "the curator settles ... every question about a decision of the curator", to reconcile; the runner did not check that a rewritten entry cites only rows that exist at the base (row 832 came after it).

## Still owed before the texts enter POSITIONS

- The curator sees the thirteen texts, each with what changed, and says yes; then `record.py apply` on `main` with `evidence/rewrite/combined.apply`, adjusted for his answers (the dependent sentences are listed per entry in each chunk's `proposals.md`).
- The judges' queue items, filed after his yes: how the team's library text is dated against a prelude design (P-26, P-37); whether P-12 names rows 470 and 731; P-85's lean; P-58's informed yes; review-queue items 215, 218, 219, 220 and 221 answered by a yes to the texts.
- Outside the entries, named by the judges and the grader: P-153's "Why" reads against the new P-26; row 816 and the conversation note say "Chase's 2012 export check" (the count is Sukyoung Ryu's, `ac0d41de0`, 2009-05-08; `5a68404fd` and `a9c625b1e` of 2012 are parentless snapshots); the specification's callout (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:62-65`) and `fortress-repo`'s `references/compiler.md` say row 412's `Object` lasts "until the switch-over"; `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` says `Any` holds "functions"; `fortress-repo`'s `references/exploring.md:16-22` lists the old later word, and its line 7 against the coordinator skill's test of a consequential choice.

His hunch that layers were mixed is right in form; the crossing was L1→L2 on 09-20 (a WD sentence kept as the reason for a compiled-path setting), not L3→L1.

71	**What he was told, and whether it changes the decision.** Told: that the compile path writes `Object` and this refuses tuples (true); that Steele switched the bound off in 2012 for the interpreter tests (true, half the story); that the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types (wrong: it puts arrows under `Object`); that "nothing in the code changes because of it" (wrong: `Shell.java:372`). Had he been told all of it, the question under P-26 would have been "is Steele's 2012 setting the team's later word on the language?", and the answer above is no. His yes rested on the tuples; the tuples decide it. The decision stands and is stronger.
72	
73	**Where the entry misstates.** "Functions" (rq 218): the WD puts arrows outside `Object`, the Types chapter inside; drop the word, as the specification's callout already does. "The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure": the switch-over ends nothing by itself; `Shell.java:372` does, and no step named it (F-289, 685 errors under the command's setting).

75	**Defaults.** P-42 stands (his; no change). The flip lands in 22c as one small rung: `Shell.java:372` to `false`, `XXXImplicitBoundAny` promoted, three pinned diagnostics rewritten, four `comprises` tests written `where [\E\]`, `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`'s premise rewritten with row 653 named, `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` given `T extends Object` with a comment naming the prelude's `||` until the switch-over (the smallest edit that keeps the test's purpose; the other way is an `XXX` test). The flip is the coordinator's to schedule (P-42 promised it), named to him because he listed it among 22c's candidates.

77	## 5. Phase 3's close: his framing is sound, and 22c carries four rungs
78	
79	- **Why the framing is sound.** J1024 §6 called phase 3 done by P-33's letter with its exit restated, and named a wider checker zero for phase 4. ### 2.3 The team's later word: the code

The code never ran the Working Draft's rule. The interpreter's library typed every integer power `RR64`, on a tower where every integer was an `RR64`, with natives that answer the integer for a nonnegative exponent and a float for a negative one (REPORT, section 6; `Int.java:222-231`). The compiled prelude typed `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32 : ZZ32`, `NN32 ^ NN32 : NN32` and `NN64 ^ NN64 : NN64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:267`, `:326`, `:385`; `.fss:744`): the exponent's type is the base's, signed where the base is, and the result is the base's type at every exponent; its negative case is the cast of `Math.pow`, 0 (row 523; row 441). Steele's `intToIntPower` is bound nowhere (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:380-398`). And the team's own tests use a signed computed exponent as an integer: `p = 2^(k-1)` then `p BITOR (p-1)` (`ProjectFortress/library_tests/ShiftTest2.fss:19-20`), `d = 2^n'` compared with a `ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/tests/zeno.fss:57`), and the library's `strToInt`, `d radix^(n-i)` summed in a `SUM[\ZZ32\]` (`fss:4540-4541`). Under the Working Draft's rule each of these is a rational.

So the later word, which outweighs the earlier text (P-26), is: an integer `^` gives the integer's own type at a signed exponent. That is the premise he took (PLAN item 58; B.2, first point). On the value at a negative exponent the code is silent, as B.2 found: a cast's by-product and an unbound helper are not a position.

## 3. The answer, case by case

| case | the tower gave | the flat design can give | by which way | at what cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. unsigned exponent (`NN32`, `NN64`) | the integer | the integer | any contract; the natives answer it today (REPORT, section 1.1; row 438) | item 58's text, nothing more |
| 2. signed computed exponent (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`) | a rational, by type, also at a nonnegative value | the rational, as R; or the integer with an error or a zero at a negative value (E, Z); or a static refusal (X) | R: `opr ^(self, b:ZZ32):QQ` and two siblings (REPORT, section 3.2) | R: 16 of 26 walk tests fail, the quick pair stops in `strToInt`, Q-walk first, 21 edits, about 32 sites of 34 (section 4.1); and it rebuilds a rule the team's code and tests never followed (section 2.3) |
| 3. numeral exponent (`16`, `-16`) | an integer for `2^3`, a rational for `10^(-16)` | one answer for both: the numeral's sign is not in its type, and under walk the numeral has no type of its own | none in the library; a signed numeral type (section 4.6, F2) plus Q-walk | reverses P-76 in part; waits for Q-walk; even then `RR64 × QQ` has no overload, so the three tests still need a float base (section 4.6) |
| 4. float or rational base | ℝ or ℚ, any exponent | the same, today | `Float`'s and `QQ`'s own `^` (section 4.2) | none |

So the whole cannot be rebuilt. The hole is case 3, and case 3 is where the team's tests are: all 11 negative-exponent sites in walk's suite write a decimal scale as `10^(-k)`, a numeral base to a numeral exponent (REPORT, section 1.3; F-247), and the two demos do the same (`ProjectFortress/demos/BiCGSTAB.fss:211`). Under the interpreter the team ran, those gave a float, by the natives (REPORT, section 1.1), which is neither the Working Draft's rational nor an integer.

## 4. The ways

Each way: the cases it covers and how; its cost in edits, the distance's sites (34 today), the quick pair, the team tests, and whether it waits for Q-walk; its evidence. The site and test figures for E, Z, R and X are the probe's, measured on the tree of 2026-10-16 at distance 49 and carried to today's 34 by subtraction (the review, section 5, lead); none was measured again here, since no way below changes the probe's text.

### 4.1 Overloads on the exponent's type

The types an exponent can have: the five integer types, of which two are unsigned, and `IntLiteral`. An overload can separate an unsigned exponent from a signed one, and a numeral from both. It cannot separate a negative `ZZ32` from a nonnegative one (section 1, fact 1).

- **R**, the Working Draft's split: unsigned and numeral exponents give the base's type, signed ones `QQ` (REPORT, section 3.2). Covers case 2 as the tower did; case 1; case 3 only after Q-walk, and then wrongly for a negative numeral, since the numeral overload is `self^(b.asNN64)` and `asNN64` refuses a negative value with "does not fit" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java:291-296`). Cost: 21 edits, 91 lines in and 29 out; `MultiplicativeRing`'s power at `NN64`, with a natural-power body on `Float`, `FloatLiteral`, `RR32` and `QQ`, or walk refuses the library at load; sites 34 to about 32, with two new ones in `FortressBuiltin` until row 445's api fix; the quick pair stops in `strToInt`, "got arg Ratio"; 10 of 26 walk tests pass; waits for Q-walk (REPORT, section 3.2; the review, section 5.3; F-247).
- **X**, Rust's way: only unsigned and numeral exponents are declared, so `2^e` with `e: ZZ32` is a static error, and every caller with a signed exponent converts it (REPORT, section 3.3). Covers cases 1 and 3; case 2 by refusal. Cost: 23 edits, 57 in and 31 out; the ring's `NN64` power and the four bodies, as R; `strToInt`, `strToFloat`, `Format.fss:95` and `:97` converted; the compiled `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32` and three compiled tests go; sites 34 to about 29, about 28 with `fail[\ZZ32\]`; the quick pair passes; 10 of 26 walk tests pass until Q-walk, 14 of them on "Ambiguous coercion"; waits for Q-walk (REPORT, section 3.3; the review, section 5.4). One cost the probe did not price: the only conversion the library has, `unsigned`, reinterprets the bits, so a caller's `radix^(unsigned(n-i))` at a negative `n-i` computes `radix^4294967295` and raises `IntegerOverflow` (section 8). X moves the sign error from the checker to a misleading overflow at run time wherever a caller converts. A checked conversion, the Working Draft's `check≥` that throws on a negative value (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:185`), is not in the library and would be new text.

### 4.2 Overloads on the base's type

Already there, and the split he is looking for, on the other operand. `Float` declares `opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64` and `opr ^(self, b:Number):RR64` (`Builtin.fss:158-161`); `QQ` declares `opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ`, with its sign test inside (`fss:641-646`). So a float or rational base takes any exponent of any sign: microGPT's own negative power is `10.0^(-5)` (REPORT, section 1.6), and `(2/3)^(-1)` is `3/2`, measured under E (REPORT, section 3.1). Covers case 4 whole. For an integer value that must be raised to a negative power, the program writes a float or rational base, `2.0^(-1)` or `(2/1)^(-1)`. Haskell makes the same split as two operators, `^` for any base at a nonnegative exponent and `^^` for a fractional base at any exponent (the review, section 4.6); Fortress has it in the base's type. Cost: no edit; the three team tests and the two demos write their scale as `10.0^(-k)` under E, Z and X alike (REPORT, section 3.1, "Cost"; the review, section 5). Does not wait for Q-walk.

### 4.3 The numeral's own declarations

Each integer type declares `opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral)` beside its `AnyIntegral` one, today `self^(b.asZZ32)` (`fss:801`; `Builtin.fss:462`, `:554`; F-79). The numeral's sign does not reach this overload: the checker types every `IntLiteralExpr` `IntLiteral` (`Misc.scala:468-469`); the compiled path folds `prefix -` on a literal into a literal of the negated value and the same type before the checker runs (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:152-153`; `.../compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:137-146`), and does not fold `^` itself (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:58-107`); unfolded, `opr -(self): IntLiteral` gives the same type (`Builtin.fss:516`). Under walk the overload is never chosen, since a numeral is an `Int` (F-74). So this way covers case 3 only as a copy of what the signed overload does: the integer under E and Z, a `QQ` under R (and a refusal of a negative numeral by accident, section 4.1). Cost: none now; after Q-walk, its body must agree with the signed one. Waits for Q-walk to matter at all.

### 4.4 The witness `typecase`, `cast`, and the run-time sign test

The library chooses by a type with `typecase`: by a static argument alone, through the witness `__thrower[\T\]` and `cast[\T\]` (`additiveIdentity`, `fss:3362-3377`; `cast`, `fss:33-37`), or by a value's run-time type over the comprised integer types (`exactValue`, `fss:398-408`; `Number`'s `=`, `fss:386-395`). Inside an arm, a sign is tested by comparison, which is the library's rule for a sign-refined subset (P-80): `QQ`'s power tests `-other > 0` (`fss:642`), the probe's `QQ` body tests `e < 0` inside each signed arm (REPORT, section 4), and the natives test `exp < 0` (`Int.java:226`). These devices give a sign-dependent value, not a sign-dependent type: the checker types a `typecase` as the join of its arms (REPORT, section 4), which for a `ZZ32` arm and a `QQ` arm is `Number`, which has no operators (section 4.5). Covers: the negative branch of E and Z, and `QQ`'s body, 4 of the 6 sites, 8 lines for 6. Does not wait for Q-walk. This is the way E and Z are built (REPORT, sections 3.1 and 4).

## 1. His question, and the three facts the coordinator gave him

His words, as the coordinator cleaned them (the brief holds the raw text):

> I need more context to make an informed decision. This seems like a consequence of flattening the numeric tower, and much of the existing library design depends on this tower. None of the options seem to fit, because it's not a one-size-fits-all kind of solution that can cover all cases. I feel we likely need a combination of several options to rebuild the original behavior of the numeric tower, but at the same time I worry that might not be possible in the current design. I would like Fable to weigh in on this. Can't we somehow use clever overloads to split the negative exponents away from the positive ones? But I guess there's no way to attempt a coercion to NN when the exponents are already ZZ… Before asking Fable: do you see where I am going with this? Is that an unreasonable direction?

The direction is reasonable, and it is the right instinct: split by type. The answer below says which types can carry the split in the flat design (the base's type, and for the exponent only an unsigned width) and which cannot (the sign of a `ZZ32`, and the sign of a numeral). The three facts the coordinator told him are checked:

1. **Overloading picks by the arguments' types, never by their values, on both paths.** Confirmed. The specification dispatches "the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time" by the arguments' dynamic types (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`); walk dispatches on run-time classes (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program"); the checker on static types. The one place the Working Draft put a value into a type was the numeral: `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, with the value `v` a static parameter (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-85`). The revival's `IntLiteral` carries none (P-76; `Misc.scala:468-469`).
2. **Nothing converts a `ZZ32` into an `NN32` implicitly.** Confirmed, and stronger than stated. `NN32` declares one coercion, from `IntLiteral` (`Builtin.fss:386`); `NN64` from `NN32` and `IntLiteral` (`fss:911-912`). The explicit conversion, `unsigned(self): NN32` on `ZZ32` (`fss:806`), reinterprets the bits: `unsigned(-1)` is `4294967295`, measured (section 8). And since a coercion is chosen by type, like an overload (`conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`), a declared `ZZ32` to `NN32` coercion could not refuse a negative value either: it would convert it as `unsigned` does. So "attempt a coercion to NN" cannot be a sign test, as he guessed.
3. **R is already a split by type.** Confirmed: an unsigned or numeral exponent gives the base's type and a signed one gives `QQ`, six declarations per integer type (REPORT, section 3.2).

One more point on his premise, "much of the existing library design depends on this tower". It does, in one sense and not in another. The library as the team wrote it rested on the integers being floats: in 2008, `trait Integral extends { StandardTotalOrder[\Integral\], RR64 }`, so the declared `RR64` of every integer power held both the integer of a nonnegative power and the float of a negative one (REPORT, section 6; row 438). It never rested on ℤ ⊂ ℚ for the power: no native ever produced a rational (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:222-231`). The flat tower removed the first (d846e3644, 2026-09-27), and the six sites are the residue (F-241). So the question is which leg of the tower, if any, to put back, and section 2 names the legs.

## 2. What the tower gave, and what it rested on

### 2.1 The Working Draft, case by case

- **An unsigned exponent.** ℕ was a synonym for ℤ≥, the nonnegative integers (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:65`), itself a subtype of ℤ and of ℚ≥ (`:37-38`). ℤ declared `opr ^(self, power: ℕ): ℤ`, "Exponentiation of an integer to a nonnegative integer power produces an integer result" (`:137`; `git show 5a68404fd:Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, lines 506-510). The result: an integer.
- **A signed computed exponent.** ℤ's power does not apply to a ℤ exponent. But ℤ extended ℚ (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:195-196`), and ℚ declared `opr ^(self, power: ℤ): ℚ#`, "Exponentiation of a rational number to an integer power produces a rational result", with `x^y = 1/(x^(-y))` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex:344-355`). So `2^n` with `n: ℤ` was a rational, by type, also when `n` held 3. To get an integer back, a program wrote a run-time check: `check≥(self): ℤ≥ throws CastError` (`basic-integers.tex:181-192`, the twelve check methods).
- **A numeral.** A numeral is digits and letters, with no sign (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`). A digits-only numeral had the type `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (`literals.tex:83-85`), so `2^3` chose ℤ's power and stayed an integer. `-16` is the prefix operator `-` applied to the numeral `16`, a ℤ, so `10^(-16)` chose ℚ's power and gave the rational 1/10^16; and `7.07 10^(-1)` was ℝ times ℚ, fine because ℚ ⊂ ℝ (`numbers.tex:36-37`).
- **A float or rational base.** ℝ's and ℚ's own powers, at any integer exponent.

### 2.2 The three legs, and where each went

The tower's answer rested on three things, and the revival set each aside by a decision of his:

- **L1, subtyping among the number types**, ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, so that a ℤ exponent reached ℚ's method and a ℚ result flowed into ℝ code. Gone with the flat tower, by the exclusion rule (P-43).
- **L2, a numeral type that carries its value**, hence its sign. Set aside for the compiler library's `IntLiteral` (P-76, "taken over the specification's unfinished numeral types").
- **L3, sign-refined types with run-time checks**, ℤ≥ and `check≥`; in the later chapter, the refinements are boolean static parameters of one trait, which the exclusion rule refuses, and "the way back is the later chapter's declaration-site variance: each flag a covariant static parameter" (`Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14-31`, `:34-45`). Superseded (P-80: "a program tests such a subset at run time"); their return waits on covariance (P-62; row 404).

## 2. The designers' word

- **The earlier word, the Working Draft.** The integers chapter declares `opr ^(self, power: NN): ZZ`: "Exponentiation of an integer to a nonnegative integer power produces an integer result" (`git show 5a68404fd:Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, lines 506-510).   - With ℤ a subtype of ℚ, an exponent typed ℤ picks ℚ's power, so 2^(−1) is 1/2.
  - A digits-only numeral had a natural type, `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-85`), so `x^2` picked ℤ's power.

- **The later word, the team's code.**
  - The interpreter's library typed every integer power `RR64` (section 6) while every integer was an `RR64`. Its natives answer the integer for a nonnegative exponent and a float for a negative one.

- **They conflict.** The earlier word gives a rational, and the later gives an integer type for every exponent. So the peers follow, in section 5.

## 3. Row 816 and P-158 (10-25 19:06 to 10-26 04:28)

**The argument, in the order he asked for it (19:35:13):**

1. *The two paths call a method differently.* Walk finds a method on the object by name at the call; the trait need not declare it. The compiled path calls through the trait's Java interface; if the trait does not declare the method, the call dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
2. *The team's two libraries each followed their path.* The compiler's prelude: the api writes `abstract loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` in `GeneratorZZ32`; the component restates `loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` with no body; the objects give the body (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:112-120`, `.fss:301-312`). The team's export check enforced it (its count written by Sukyoung Ryu, `ac0d41de0`, 2009-05-08; first written here as Chase's of 2012, `5a68404fd`, a parentless snapshot): a component trait with fewer members than its api trait is refused. The interpreter's library, written for walk and never compiled by the team, sometimes leaves an api's `abstract` member out of the component's trait (`String`'s `split`), and walk does not care.
3. *What the revival changed.* When the checker read the interpreter's library, the team's check refused 12 such members. Two ways: (a) add the 12 declarations to the components, the compiled library's way; (b) weaken the check. Climb batch 21b's rung E took (b) (`031c38bbc`), from a misreading of `apis.tex` ("includes definitions for all declarations other than … abstract" read as "needs no member", where it says "needs no body"). The chain: an Opus ways worker of 10-20 (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, "4i", "Decision: none, since it is the text's own rule"); the export probe of 10-23 built it; batch 21's planner made it fork 20 with the default "the team's own text"; its Fable review and I passed it as not consequential; rung E built it; its skeptic found the `NoSuchMethodError` after the build; the 21b review kept it as "it cannot happen yet"; batch 22 carried it as question 1 and I launched batch 22 at about 02:01 on 10-24 without sending him the question. No document before the change mentions `NoSuchMethodError`. Root cause: one sentence misread; nobody read the code it changed (the team's deliberate count) or asked what a compiled call does; the change cleared errors, which was the batch's goal.
4. *The fix (his option 2).* Restore the team's count; add 12 bodyless declarations to five component traits (`String` 7: `depth`, `isBalanced`, `verify`, `rangeContains`, `balanced`, `splitWithOffsets`, `split`; `Range`'s `isEmpty`; `ReadableArray`'s `opr[_:TrivialOpenRange]`; `ActualReduction`'s `empty` and `join`; `AnyMaybe`'s `holds`). No body, not an empty body: an empty body makes the method concrete, and then no object must define it.

**His decision:** option 2 (19:06:08 on 10-25); his reason (04:28:41 on 10-26): "by the standing position that later team's work supersedes earlier one, we take the compiled path's way over the walk library's. That's why 21b should have chosen (a), not weaken the check — we must reverse this." Recorded as P-158 (`edbd0d4f5`, reason `5da8144e4`); F-282 and row 816 rewritten; PLAN's phase 4 line "Row 816's repair". At 07:30:36 he placed the repair in climb batch 22c (section 6).

## 4. The library route and its premise (10-26, 04:31 to 05:25)

- Ask 2 (is phase 3 done, its exit restated) led to his statement of the goal (04:47:50): "The whole point of the switch-over is to avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library. The revival is continuing the development of the type checker, so that it would accept the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses." P-37 lacks this reason; it goes in with the rewrites (section 8).
- The history, read in full at his insistence (`postmortem-2026-09-19/direction-history-transcripts.md`, `two-libraries.md`, `library-route-judgement.md`): on 09-15 he did not know there were two libraries; at 23:51 on 09-15 he asked "Couldn't the path forward be just to use the FortressLibrary for compiler as well?"; a probe (00:13 on 09-16) found 95% of the library plain Fortress, but desugaring and code generation were never reached; the coordinator put the fork twice as "not needed yet" (09-16) and on 09-17 chose the porting route for him, unpriced, and he accepted an order of steps; on 09-20 the post-mortem found this; his words "we need to unify this. into single library", "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it" (P-37). Maessen's 2008 comment calls the switch a "hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (its reason Java imports, not the checker); the team left no plan to end the split and grew the prelude until June 2012; the specification knows one library.
- **The other 40 components** (624 errors, 25 crashes, F-290) are outside phase 3's twelve. He agreed the plan never meant them for phase 3 ("Of course"), but the goal is the fuller library. My view, his to confirm: they do not block the switch-over; they block P-12's step (walk runs the checker), so each reaches zero before that step or before the first program that needs it.
- At 05:25:27 he doubted the premise ("whether I made a good and well informed decision, or a mistake"), named the bound as a possible linchpin, and asked to re-verify the foundational tenets: the foundations review (section 5).

## 5. The foundations review (approved 06:11:21)

**Scope, nine tenets, each ground filed by the three layers:** 1 the goal (P-7, P-8); 2 the team's later word (P-26); 3 one library (P-37), premise that the compiled path can run it, not only check it; 4 the bound `Any` (P-42); 5 the exclusion rule and flat numbers (P-43); 6 the phase order (P-33); 7 unboxed doubles and `double[]` (P-17, P-84); 8 the natives' form (P-58); 9 walk runs the checker (P-12, P-59).

**Step 1, done.**
- `reviews/foundations/bound-archaeology.md` (`ab2ee0c29`): the Working Draft's `Object` sentence is not in 1.0 (2008), first in bulk imports of 2009-11; later team texts split (Welterweight, the 2011 paper, POPL 2019 p. 11:9 give `Any`; Naden 2012 calls `Object` "the distinguished top type"; a 2008 commit left "either Object or Any" open). Steele wrote the compiled path's `Object` default on 2012-05-28 (`91e71e62e`, "amazingly, this was not yet implemented", writing `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and tests that take tuples, arrows or `()`), turned it off on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass" (`c61723f61`), and made it a setting, on for the compiled path, on 05-30 (`afb02f41d`). No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. `java.lang.Object` maps to Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`). On 09-29 he was told the compiled path writes `Object` and that Steele switched it off for the interpreter tests, but not that Steele switched it on for the compiled path as the language's rule; two statements of mine that day were wrong (the sentence's date; "the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types").
- `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md` (`4b3d91cb4`): under `Any`, tuple and arrow static arguments compile, load and run (same classes and bytecode as with `extends Any` written); `()` dies with `AbstractMethodError` under both bounds (row 339); a new defect: a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter dies with `ClassCastException` (`CodeGen.java:6250-6263`), both bounds, no row yet; under `Object`, `id((3, 4))` compiles as `id(3)` (row 691); `ant testQuick` under `Any`: 12 failures in 10 compiler tests, all test-side; the switch is one small rung. Its findings for the ledger and FACTS, and its two questions (when `Any` reaches `fortress compile`; `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC`), wait for the judgement.

**Step 2, done.** `reviews/foundations/tenets-evidence.md` (`6c6437dfc`), read in full. Its new finds: the team's JVM type mapping relies on the exclusion rule (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:125`); the prelude's flattening of 2009 (`6896886fb`) is a code-generator commit with no stated reason; P-26's list of the later word counts layer-2 code (the prelude's flattening, the export check, the powers) as the language's word; "specialization kept" names a layer-1 thing in P-26 and a layer-2 thing in `exploring.md:20`; walk cannot run the checker as set (Scala off, the Java checker gone, no case for `CoercionInvocation`), so P-12's "small change" is not small; his class-loader lean of 09-20 for the unboxed store was never recorded; he was told on 09-19 that stamping "only renames" (no generic instance holds a `double[]`) and on 09-24 that "unboxing will build on it"; his informed yes to P-58 is still owed. Its tensions: P-37's ruling called the prelude "what they could do behind the JVM wall" (layer 2) while P-43's "Why" calls it "the team's last record of the Fortress way" (layer 1).

**The prelude-lens sweep, running** (his yes 07:36:39; `reviews/foundations/prelude-lens.md` when it returns). His worry (07:30:36): where the two libraries differed, did we port the compiler prelude's legitimate later designs into the one library (as the flat numbers), or just extend the checker to accept whatever the interpreter library wrote? No review had swept for it: the phase 3 audit's Part B judged library changes against the interpreter library's own text and the specification and left the prelude out; no review compared checker changes with the prelude's way. Caution: the prelude was "stripped-down minimalist … for first crack at compilation", with parts the team called "bogus" and a "bogo-trait": the sweep sorts each prelude choice into a deliberate design (commit, author, date) or a bootstrap stub. Places we took the prelude's design: P-43, P-76, P-77, P-47; one where we did the opposite: row 816.

**Step 3, next:** the Fable judgement on step 1, step 2 and the sweep (his go of 06:11:21 includes it), then a page for him by an Opus writer. Its brief must name the exclusion-fork notes directly (section 7).

## 6. His framing of the phase (07:30:36)

This is the phase 3 exit review. So far the tenets hold. If the judgement holds them, no major re-evaluation of direction is needed; phase 3 closes with one more batch, **climb batch 22c** (or more if needed), for the rungs left, to exit phase 3 cleanly. Candidates: row 816's repair (P-158); the 9 operator headers that differ between api and component (row 782); `List`'s two unchecked imports (`CovariantCollection`, `OneShotFlag`); the bound `Any` for `fortress compile` (the probe's one small rung). Batch 23 (the natives) follows. This takes the place of ask 2's options (phase 3 done with its exit restated, or open until the wider zero); P-33's phase 3 text is rewritten after the judgement. The earlier asks 3 to 8 (P-58's informed yes; P-155 to cover the export check; P-75 withdrawn; his texts to correct; rq 35 and rq 230; batch 23's go) are still open, after the review.

## 7. The flat numbers: my framing corrected (07:46:17)

I had framed the judge's question as whether the prelude's flat numbers are a design of the language or a JVM measure. He corrected me: the record's digging decided the flat tower, and I was wrong. The grounds on record: the exclusion rule in the team's language texts (the 2011 paper, `exclusion.tick:141-152`; the 2012 Types chapter, `types.tick:355-376`; Naden 2012, "blanket … for the semantic benefits and the simplicity"; POPL 2019 keeps it); under the rule a nested tower is impossible (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral` at different arguments); the Working Draft says the number types "are mutually exclusive" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`); Steele's 2016 talk shows a flat tower; the checker relies on the rule (F-44) and so does the JVM mapping (`TypeMapping.tex:125`); routes A, B and C weighed 09-22 to 09-24 (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`, `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md`, `reviews/mie-probes/`), A chosen 09-24; reviews D4 (09-29), the POPL recheck and V5 (10-23) keep it. What is open is narrower: P-43's stated reason, "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way", is the weakest ground and not his words (rq 219). The judge's real question for P-37: when does a design of the compiler's prelude bind the one library? My answer, for the judge to weigh: when the team's later word on the language backs it, as the exclusion rule backs the flat numbers.

## 8. The POSITIONS rewrites and the trap test (approved 07:42:15 and 07:48:49)

- He said yes (07:42:15) to rewording P-37 and P-26. My drafts of 07:39:43 (P-37: his reason plus "a deliberate design of the compiler's prelude, the team's later work (P-26), goes into the one library … a stub … does not count"; P-26: "a ground is weighed in its own layer … does not decide a question in another") pull against each other, since the prelude is layer-2 work; so the text waits for the judgement. Rewrite scope: P-26, P-37, and every entry the judgement says bends or lacks its real reason (likely P-43's "Why", P-42's grounds, P-33's phase 3 text).
- **The plan (his yes 07:48:49):** after the Fable judgement, an Opus worker writes 4 trap scenarios from the old entries and his words, before the new text exists; the scenarios are the coordinator's forks (planning a batch, choosing a probe, weighing a trade-off) where the old text leads the wrong way; the readers act as the coordinating session (coordinator skill and record loaded); the clarity workflow rewrites the entries (writer, cold reader, fidelity check, one fix, judge; `tools/record-clarity/README.md`); the record-test kit runs the test (`process-engineering/record-test/README.md`): one Opus reader in a copy with the old entries, one with the new, a blind Opus grader; a failed trap is fixed and rerun; nothing enters POSITIONS until it passes. Keep it small.

If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait called,
say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises} clause,

- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.

- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.

- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.

- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. Every binding still names a glue class. Row 796: walk loads a binding's string only as a glue class. Row 309: the compiled path has no counterpart of `builtinPrimitive`.

- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3, the compiled checker reports no error on the interpreter's whole library (the distance to the switch-over at zero; F-53 defines it and holds its value); phase 4, the switch-over, first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

9:  - Tuples, now: the ways note's way 1b. Each element type of a pair or triple is bounded by `StandardPartialOrder` (the library's own device for the tuple comparison it typed, `PCMP`, and for the tuple reductions); `Comparison` gains the lazy `LEXICO` that `TotalComparison` already has and the team's compiler prelude declares; each `typecase` gains an `Unordered` clause. 17 sites clear. Pairs of floats, integers, strings, characters, booleans and lists keep their values. Neither model program compares a tuple or a list.
19:- A *tuple* is `(a, b)` or `(a, b, c)`. A *type parameter* is the `A` in `opr <[\A,B\](t1:(A,B), t2:(A,B))`. A *bound* is a requirement written on it, `A extends StandardPartialOrder[\A\]`; without one, the parameter's implicit bound is `Any`, the top of the type system (POSITIONS, "The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`").

So no bound on a trait admits a pair as an element of a pair. Whatever bound is chosen, the pair of pairs is lost unless the type system changes or the check moves to run time.
